title: Can buyers bring buyers?
principle: A loop where buyers bring buyers beats paying for each one.

screens.text: Let me tell you about Hotmail. In July 1996, Sabeer Bhatia, who grew up in India, and Jack Smith started a free email service on the web. They had little money for ads. So at the bottom of every email, they added one line: "Get your free email at Hotmail."

screens.prompt: Every email a user sent carried that line. What do you think happened next?

options.label: It grew slowly, as small ads do
Users complained, so it was removed
A million joined within six months

screens.why: A million people joined within six months. Every email a user sent was a small ad, read by a friend who could join for free. Then that friend's emails did the same. In December 1997, Microsoft bought Hotmail.

screens.title: Growth loops
screens.text: This is a growth loop: each buyer's use brings in the next buyer. Ads stop the day you stop paying, but a loop keeps going. Growth teams measure it with a number called the K-factor: new buyers for each buyer. If 10 buyers bring 5 more, K is 0.5.

screens.prompt: 20 families order cakes in April. Their party guests bring 6 new families in May. What's your K-factor?
screens.why: Exactly. 6 new families ÷ 20 buyers = 0.3. Each family brings about a third of a new one. That helps, but below 1 the loop can't grow on its own, so you still need other roads in.

wrong.b: You did 20 ÷ 6. Flip it: new families ÷ buyers. 6 ÷ 20 = 0.3.
wrong.c: 6 is the number of new families. K-factor is new families for each buyer: 6 ÷ 20 = 0.3.

screens.title: Now look at your business
screens.text: Hotmail's line rode on every email, and your cake rides into every party. It's late May. About 15 guests see each birthday cake you make, and some ask the family, "Who made this?" But most families can't remember your name or number.

screens.prompt: I'll show you six ideas. For each one, tell me: does it build a loop, or pay for each new buyer?

items.text: A small card with your number in every cake box
A thank-you note in each box, asking them to share your number
₹2,000 to a food blogger for one post
Your WhatsApp number printed on the cake board
Flyers handed out at the market

screens.why: Well sorted. A loop rides on something your buyer already does: opening a box, sharing cake with guests. Paid ways bring buyers only while you keep paying.

screens.prompt: True or false: once you have a loop, you never need to spend money on finding customers.

options.label: True: the loop does all the work
False: you still need other ways in

screens.why: False. Most loops have a K-factor below 1. Each round of buyers brings a smaller round, so the loop slows down unless new buyers keep coming in from somewhere else.

wrong.a: Only if K is above 1, which is rare. With K at 0.3, 20 families bring 6, those 6 bring about 2, and the loop slows down. You still need other roads in.

screens.prompt: A happy family says, "We'll tell all our friends about you!" How do you know if your loop is working?

options.label: Ask how many friends they told

screens.why: Right. Remember Unit 2: praise is not proof. Ask each new buyer, "How did you hear about us?" and count. That's how you know your K-factor.

wrong.a: Kind words are nice, but they prove nothing. Remember Unit 2: praise is not proof. Count orders that came from their friends.
wrong.b: "We told ten friends" is still just words. Remember Unit 2: praise is not proof. Count orders that came from their friends.

screens.setup: It's the end of May. Cards in boxes now bring 6 new families from every 20 orders. You have ₹4,000 to spend on getting more. Each cake leaves you ₹450. Count first cakes only.
screens.question: How do you spend it?

options.label: Boost Instagram reels with all ₹4,000
options.outcome: The ads bring 10 families. Their first cakes leave you ₹4,500, so you're only ₹500 up. When the ads stop, so do the new families.
options.why: Ads can pay, and you'll check that sum soon. But you paid for each buyer, so the new families stopped the day the ads ended.
options.better: Give ₹50 off to the family and ₹50 off to each friend who orders, so buyers bring buyers.

options.label: ₹50 off for the family, and ₹50 off for each friend
options.outcome: Families start sharing your number. 20 orders now bring 12 new families, not 6. The 6 extra families leave you ₹2,700. The ₹50 discounts cost ₹1,200, so you're ₹1,500 up. And the new families start bringing friends too.
options.why: You made sharing worth it, so your K-factor doubled from 0.3 to 0.6, and the loop keeps paying next month.

options.label: Print nicer boxes with your name on every order
options.outcome: The boxes cost ₹4,000. Guests admire them, but few ask for your number. 20 orders bring 7 new families, just 1 more than before. You're ₹3,550 down.
options.why: A nice box gave guests no reason to order. It cost a lot and barely moved your K-factor.
options.better: Give ₹50 off to the family and ₹50 off to each friend who orders, so buyers bring buyers.

screens.text: A growth ___ makes each buyer bring the next one, so you don't ___ for every new buyer.
screens.why: Exactly. Hotmail's line rode on every email. Your cards and referral offer ride on every cake.

summary: A growth loop: each buyer's use brings in the next buyer. Word of mouth is the oldest loop.
K-factor = new buyers ÷ buyers who brought them. Below 1, you still need other roads in.
Make sharing easy and worth it, then count where new buyers came from.

cards.front: 30 buyers bring 15 new buyers. What's the K-factor?
cards.back: 15 ÷ 30 = 0.5. Each buyer brings half a new one.

cards.front: Which builds a loop for a tiffin service?
options: A referral offer for both sides
cards.back: A loop rides on what buyers already do. Ads stop when the money stops.

cards.front: Your K-factor is 0.4. Can you stop all other ways of finding buyers?
cards.back: Below 1, each round brings a smaller round. You still need other roads in.
